opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that at the frontier, the things that really matter can't be validated quickly. When you train a model at K2's scale, a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts, you're making a lot of bets at once: the architecture, the optimizer, the data recipe, how you approach agentic capabilities. Each of those has to be validated on its own before you can trust it at full scale, because one full training run is extremely expensive. You don't get many shots.

Take the optimizer. We spent a long time on Muon. On paper it had very attractive properties, especially token efficiency, and token efficiency matters a lot to us because high-quality data is becoming the real bottleneck. But going from "this works on a small model" to "this is stable for a trillion-parameter run over many trillions of tokens" is a huge gap. We ran into problems like attention logits blowing up, which you only see clearly at certain scales. Solving that, which eventually became what we call MuonClip, took many rounds of small-scale experiments, then medium-scale, then checking whether the conclusions still held. That process is slow by nature. You have to be patient and rigorous, otherwise you end up building on something that collapses halfway through the big run.

The second reason is scaling laws in a broader sense. Many conclusions are scale-dependent. Something that looks good on a small model might disappear or even reverse when you scale up. So a lot of the preparation is building a reliable experimental ladder, a set of smaller setups whose results actually predict what happens at the target scale. Building that ladder and trusting it is itself a research project.

The third part is the data and the agentic side. We wanted K2 to be good at using tools and doing multi-step tasks, not just chatting. That requires a lot of infrastructure: synthesizing environments, generating trajectories, designing reward signals that aren't easily hacked. None of that comes for free, and you can't really rush it, because if the data is subtly wrong, the model learns the wrong behaviors very efficiently.

So for me the long preparation isn't a cost to minimize. It's where most of the real work happens. The final training run is almost the visible tip. What determines whether it succeeds is whether you've done the slow, careful validation beforehand. And honestly, I think that's also where a smaller team can compete: not by out-spending anyone, but by being more thoughtful about which bets to make and more disciplined about validating them.

r001.rationale: The response says Muon needed testing from small models through medium-scale experiments to confirm stability at trillion-parameter scale.

r002.rationale: It states that attention logits blowing up became clear only at certain scales.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that K2 wasn't really a matter of just scaling up what we already had. A lot of the core things we wanted to put into it needed to be validated at small scale first, and that validation itself takes a long time.

Take the optimizer, for example. We spent a very long time on Muon. The question wasn't just whether Muon works on a small model, it was whether it stays stable and keeps its advantage as you scale. If you push the scale up and suddenly the loss spikes, or the gradients blow up, you've basically wasted an enormous amount of compute. So we had to run a lot of scaling-law experiments, work out things like weight decay and the QK-clip trick, and only when we were confident that these held across several orders of magnitude could we commit to the full run.

Same with the data side. Token efficiency matters a lot to us, because high-quality data is finite. We had to figure out how to rephrase and augment data so that each token delivers more learning without overfitting. That's not something you can test cheaply on a huge model, so again, lots of small and medium-scale experiments.

And then there's the agentic capability, which was really the thing we cared about most. To train that, you need an environment to synthesize tool-use data, you need verification, you need reinforcement learning infrastructure that can scale. Building all of that from scratch and making sure it actually produces generalizable ability, not just memorized trajectories, takes months.

So if you add it up, the actual pretraining run is relatively short compared to the time spent making sure every component is right before you press the button. A trillion-parameter run is expensive enough that you only get one real shot. That's why I'd rather have a long preparation cycle and a clean run than rush and have to restart.

r001.rationale: The response says they ran scaling-law experiments and validated the optimizer and related choices across several orders of magnitude before committing to the trillion-parameter run.

r002.rationale: It explains that scaling up can reveal instability, such as loss spikes or exploding gradients, and that Muon’s stability and advantage must be checked at larger scales.

astra-6.text:
Because you’re not just validating one idea. You’re building a whole system, and you need to understand whether the different parts work together. A promising result in a small experiment doesn’t necessarily mean the same approach will work when you scale it up.

So there are several rounds of work: you form a hypothesis, run experiments, examine the failures, and revise the approach. Then you have to validate it at a larger scale. If you change several things at once, it can also be difficult to tell what actually caused the improvement.

That’s why the preparation takes time. Before committing to a large training run, you want enough evidence that the key decisions are sound. The final run is the visible part, but a lot of the research and uncertainty reduction happens before it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that research and validation happen on different timescales. You can come up with an idea fairly quickly, but establishing that it works—and that the improvement will hold when you scale it up—takes much longer. You need to run experiments, understand why something succeeds or fails, and then use those results to decide what to try next. Those steps are sequential; you can’t compress everything simply by adding more resources.

For K2, the preparation is about reducing uncertainty before committing to the largest training run. It’s not enough to see a promising result once. You need enough evidence to trust the direction, and building that confidence requires repeated experimentation. So what looks like a single model release is really the culmination of a much longer research cycle.
